rollups.text: Geometry software and visualization tools Jamie used or considered: GeoGebra and GeoGebra 3D for modeling and checking geometry (2024-01-10 onward); NonEuclid and Poincaré-disk applets for hyperbolic geometry (2024-01-24); Wolfram Alpha for checking hyperbolic-trigonometric calculations (2024-01-24); Spherical Easel for spherical geometry (2024-01-10); physical globe or spherical balloon with string and pins for spherical-triangle visualization (2024-01-10).

Jamie repeatedly studied Euclidean geometry, hyperbolic geometry, spherical geometry, Euclid’s parallel postulate, triangle angle sums and area, curvature, and Poincaré-disk geodesics (2024-01-10 onward). Historical figures discussed included Euclid, Carl Friedrich Gauss, Nikolai Lobachevsky, János Bolyai, and Bernhard Riemann; Jamie planned to read Lobachevsky’s 1829 paper during 2024-01-15..2024-01-21 and Riemann’s 1854 lecture during 2024-01-29..2024-02-04.

Jamie prefers foundational, clear, step-by-step explanations with equations, examples, visual aids, diagrams, and interactive tools; Jamie values worked examples, intermediate checks, GeoGebra verification, and everyday-object visualizations. Jamie specifically requested detailed explanations of triangle angle sums and visual aids for hyperbolic-geometry problems (2024-01-10..2024-02-07).

Jamie’s non-Euclidean geometry study progressed from introductory Euclidean parallel-line problems and comparisons of Euclidean, hyperbolic, and spherical geometry (2024-01-10), through curvature, triangle angle sums, spherical excess, and Poincaré-disk models (2024-01-10..2024-01-24), to repeated practice with hyperbolic and spherical triangle calculations (2024-02-07). Jamie sought help with GeoGebra constructions throughout; many assistant-provided geodesic constructions and numerical examples were later recorded as unreliable, so they should not be treated as validated solutions.

Jamie repeatedly worked on the hyperbolic triangle with side lengths 1, 1.5, and 2: on 2024-01-24 Jamie asked for its angles, angle sum, and area, but received inconsistent calculations, including an incorrect estimate near 120°; subsequent replies continued to vary. On 2024-02-07 the assistant gave angles approximately 19.4°, 35.6°, and 93.0°, totaling about 148°, and Jamie later said the worked law-of-cosines example helped. The successive key dates span 14 days; the reported results across the discussion are not all reliable.

Jamie studied spherical-triangle area from angular excess: on 2024-01-10 Jamie worked with angle triples such as 80°, 60°, 70°; on 2024-02-07 Jamie asked about area formulas for a unit sphere and other radii, practiced examples including 90°, 80°, 70° and 100°, 50°, 60°, and confirmed the rule that excess in radians is multiplied by r². Jamie reported completing 7 spherical-triangle problems at 90% average accuracy on 2024-02-07. The recorded period is 28 days.

Recorded geometry-practice results include three Euclidean parallel-line problems at 80% (2024-01-10), six Euclidean parallel-line problems at 88% (2024-01-10), four Euclidean triangle-property problems with 3/4 correct (2024-01-10), five hyperbolic problems with 4/5 correct (2024-01-24), six hyperbolic triangle problems averaging 83% (2024-01-24 and 2024-02-07), a later hyperbolic accuracy report of 89% (2024-01-24), and seven spherical-triangle problems averaging 90% (2024-02-07). These are separate reported practice results, not necessarily comparable assessments.
Jamie reported improving speed on hyperbolic-triangle problems from 25 minutes per problem to 18 minutes per problem on 2024-01-24, a reduction of 7 minutes (about 28%).

Jamie’s stated study plans changed in scope: an initial plan was five triangle-angle-sum problems across three sessions (2024-01-10); a later plan was five problems across three sessions spanning Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometry, while the assistant’s proposed outline actually listed six (2024-01-10). Jamie later sought a plan for eight spherical-triangle problems across four sessions (2024-01-24).

Geometry and astronomy software Jamie used, tried, or was advised to use: GeoGebra for hyperbolic geodesics and spherical models (2024-02-07, 2024-02-21, 2024-03-06); Cinderella, Mathematica, Geometer’s Sketchpad, and Cabri Geometry as suggested alternatives (2024-02-07); Python with Matplotlib, NumPy, and scipy.integrate.quad for plotting and numerical integration (2024-02-21, 2024-03-06); Wolfram Alpha for checking distances (2024-02-21); Stellarium for visualizing star positions and checking angular separations (2024-03-20).

Recurring spherical-triangle examples Jamie explored: a unit-sphere triangle with interior angles 100°, 50°, and 60° has angle sum 210°, spherical excess π/6, and area π/6 ≈ 0.5236 (2024-02-07, 2024-02-21, 2024-03-06, 2024-03-20); the three-right-angle octant triangle has area π/2 ≈ 1.5708 on the unit sphere (2024-02-21, 2024-03-06). Jamie also repeatedly asked about sides 60°, 70°, and 80°; responses sometimes incorrectly treated those side lengths as interior angles, so the area and angle values for that side-length example remain unresolved (2024-02-07, 2024-02-21, 2024-03-20).

Recurring hyperbolic half-plane example: for points (1,1) and (4,2), the geodesic is the semicircle (x−3)²+y²=5, centered at (3,0) with radius √5 (2024-02-21, 2024-03-06). The distance formula gives arcosh(3.5), approximately 1.925; numerous responses instead reported inconsistent incorrect approximations, including 1.2566 and 1.7627 (2024-02-21, 2024-03-06, 2024-03-20). Jamie repeatedly requested calculations, derivations, plotting, and computational checks for this example.

Jamie’s study of non-Euclidean geometry began with foundational questions about spherical and hyperbolic triangles, geodesics, curvature, and visualizations (2024-02-07). Jamie then explored the Poincaré half-plane metric, geodesic semicircles and vertical lines, distance formulas, numerical integration, and comparisons with the disk model (2024-02-21; 14 days after the initial study date). On 2024-03-06, Jamie continued with spherical geodesic lengths, vector dot products, and hyperbolic geodesic questions, reporting a plan to solve seven problems in the disk and half-plane models over the next three weeks, approximately through 2024-03-27 (14 days after the February 21 session).

Jamie’s spherical-geodesic work progressed from central angles and arc lengths to vector methods and astronomy applications. On 2024-03-06, Jamie practiced converting central angles to lengths, using dot products to find angles, and comparing vector algebra with the spherical law of cosines; Jamie reported completing six spherical-geodesic problems with 95% average accuracy and reducing average solving time to 12 minutes per problem. On 2024-03-20, Jamie applied spherical geometry to right ascension and declination, star separations, great-circle routes, and celestial navigation (14 days later). Jamie also used Stellarium to visualize star positions and check angular-separation calculations.

Jamie reported several learning-progress measures: hyperbolic-triangle average accuracy was 89% on 2024-02-07; spherical-triangle-area quiz accuracy was 92% on 2024-02-07, although Jamie also said that day they had never completed a spherical-triangle problem and remained confused; geodesic-length accuracy was reported as 92% after five problems on 2024-02-21, and later as 95% after five problems that day, alongside a separate statement that no half-plane geodesic-length problem had yet been completed; spherical-geodesic accuracy was 95% after six problems on 2024-03-06. These reports concern different problem types or are internally inconsistent, so they do not establish a single comparable accuracy trend.

Jamie reported changes in problem-solving time: on 2024-02-21, a goal of reducing average geodesic-problem time from 30 minutes to 20 minutes; on 2024-03-06, spherical-geodesic average time had improved from 22 minutes to 15 minutes, and later that day Jamie reported 12 minutes per spherical-geodesic problem. These are separate time reports and may refer to different problem sets.

Jamie’s stated preferences became increasingly specific: Jamie wanted visualizations for spherical-triangle questions (2024-02-07), preferred combining analytical formulas with computational verification for geodesic calculations (2024-02-21), and explicitly requested vector-algebra explanations rather than purely trigonometric methods for spherical-geodesic calculations (2024-03-06).

Mathematical visualization and astronomy software Jamie used, explored, or considered: GeoGebra 3D for spherical triangles, geodesics, and hyperbolic constructions (2024-03-20; 2024-04-03; 2024-04-17); Stellarium for visualizing celestial positions and star paths (2024-03-20; 2024-04-03); KaleidoTile for hyperbolic tessellations and tile measurements (2024-04-03; 2024-04-17); Mathematica for geodesic simulations and tessellation modeling (2024-04-17).

M.C. Escher works discussed in connection with geometry and art: Circle Limit III, whose fish tessellate the Poincaré disk and appear smaller near its boundary (2024-04-03); Ascending and Descending, discussed as an impossible staircase (2024-04-03); Metamorphosis II, discussed in relation to symmetry and transformation (2024-04-03); Sphere with Angels and Devils, cited in a comparison of spherical and hyperbolic art (2024-04-03).

Jamie’s study of non-Euclidean geometry and visualization tools: Jamie said the hyperbolic-geometry study began 2024-02-21 (2024-04-03); by 2024-03-20, Jamie was applying spherical geometry to astronomy and reported completing astronomy-geometry exercises (2024-03-20); on 2024-04-03, Jamie explored Poincaré models, tessellations, symmetry groups, Escher, and visualization tools while preparing for a quiz; on 2024-04-17, Jamie continued practicing spherical and hyperbolic geometry, using GeoGebra 3D, KaleidoTile, and Mathematica and asking how to validate software-assisted solutions. The documented interval from the stated study start to the latest dated activity is 56 days.

Jamie’s digital hyperbolic-tessellation project: on 2024-04-03, Jamie wanted to model a tessellation with 7-fold rotational symmetry, use software, avoid overlaps, and understand how hyperbolic distance and symmetry groups generate tiles; Jamie had used KaleidoTile and sought an artistic, visual approach. On 2024-04-17, Jamie was still working on a 7-fold Poincaré-disk tessellation, wanted to measure tile areas and compare them with theory, and was also creating KaleidoTile models with 5-fold symmetry. The recorded project spans 14 days; rotational symmetry alone does not determine a tessellation’s tile area.

Reported geometry-study results and changes: on 2024-03-20, Jamie reported 5 astronomy problems averaging 88% and separately 5 correct out of 6 astronomy-geometry problems; on 2024-04-03, Jamie said a quiz score had risen to 90% and reported 4/5 on hyperbolic-art problems; on 2024-04-17, Jamie reported software-assisted spherical-geometry accuracy increasing from 78% to 92%. These are separate reported sets or measures, not one continuous score series.

Repeated practice on a unit sphere: on 2024-04-03, Jamie checked five central angles—60°, 90°, 120°, 150°, and 180°—and their corresponding geodesic lengths; all five calculations were confirmed correct. On 2024-04-17, Jamie returned to the 90° separation example, whose unit-sphere geodesic length is π/2 ≈ 1.5708.

Cities used in spherical-distance examples: Istanbul (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); Ankara (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); New York City (2024-05-01); Los Angeles (2024-05-01); Chicago (2024-05-01); Izmir (2024-05-15); Antalya (2024-05-15).

Mathematical and visualization tools recurring in Jamie’s geometry work: GeoGebra and GeoGebra 3D (2024-04-17, 2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); KaleidoTile (2024-04-17, 2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); Python (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); Excel (2024-05-15); Mathematica (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15).

Distance methods Jamie repeatedly studied or applied: spherical law of cosines (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); haversine formula (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); hyperbolic distance formulas in the Poincaré disk and upper half-plane (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15); great-circle geodesics and distance (2024-05-01, 2024-05-15).

GPS and spherical-distance learning timeline: On 2024-05-01 Jamie worked through spherical-law-of-cosines and haversine calculations for GPS coordinates, Earth modeled with radius 6,371 km, navigation, numerical stability, and formula selection; requested step-by-step methods and precision guidance. On 2024-05-15 Jamie continued with Istanbul–Ankara examples, online verification, distances among Turkish cities, and real-time navigation/app implementation. The recorded period spans 14 days. Assistant calculations across the discussions were sometimes inconsistent or inaccurate; the records distinguish those claims from verified values.

Hyperbolic-tiling growth project timeline: On 2024-05-15 Jamie explored exponential tile-growth models, compared empirical counts with analytical derivations, asked about curvature, tile density, and fitting N(r)=N₀e^(kr), and sought beginner-friendly, step-by-step fitting explanations. Jamie reported counts of 5, 15, and 45 at radii 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3; also supplied a separate model with N₀=5 and k≈3.5, which does not match those counts. Jamie discussed Excel and KaleidoTile for collecting and analyzing tiling data, asked how to make counts reproducible, and later presented a conjecture and findings in an online seminar, receiving constructive feedback. The recorded sequence occurs within one day; no elapsed days between the dated steps are established.

Jamie reported GPS-distance problem-solving time improving from 20 minutes per problem to 12 minutes, then to 10 minutes: 8 minutes faster overall, a 40% reduction from the initial time. The 20-to-12-minute report and the 10-minute report were both dated 2024-05-01; their precise order within that date is not established.

Jamie reported completing 6 real-world spherical-geometry problems with a score of 6/6 on 2024-05-01, and 4 hyperbolic-growth exploration problems with a score of 4/4 on 2024-05-15. These are two separately reported perfect-score sets.

On 2024-05-15 Jamie reported hyperbolic-tile counts of 5 within radius 0.1, 15 within radius 0.2, and 45 within radius 0.3. The three counts fit the stated exponential curve N(r)=1.667e^(10.986r) at those radii, as recorded in the discussion.
